items.title: Against the wall of complexity: human cognition, political decision-making, and human-AI collaboration
items.abstract: In 2014, the report A World That Counts, commissioned by the United Nations Secretary-General, argued that better access to high-quality data would improve public decision-making to address major global challenges more effectively (Independent Expert Advisory Group on a Data Revolution for Sustainable Development [IEAG], 2014). Since then, data availability has increased substantially, yet the corresponding benefits for public decision-making remain mixed (Fischer et al., 2025). If the difficulties political systems face in addressing contemporary problems persist despite this abundance, data availability cannot be the whole explanation. Policy processes and outcomes also depend on political pressures, institutional rules and interactions among policy actors, limited administrative capacity, and uncertainty about policy problems and their solutions (Howlett et al., 2015). These influences increasingly operate within complex systems, which may amplify the demands each of them creates (Fernández-i-Marín et al., 2024). We focus here on the cognitive processes through which policymakers interpret information, form judgments and make decisions under these demands. We define policymakers as individuals exercising decision-making responsibilities within governance systems, from the local to the supranational level. Following Cairney and Weible (2017) in viewing policymaking as imperfect cognition operating in complex contexts, we contend that the interaction between cognitive limits and rising systemic complexity is an important source of difficulty in policymakers' judgments and decisions. To support this thesis, we draw on research in complex systems, cognitive psychology and decision science, before examining how systems thinking, simulations and human-AI collaboration can help mitigate these limitations. We conclude by arguing for humility about what can be predicted and controlled in complex policy systems (Jalonen, 2025).Contemporary societies have become more complex as digitalization and globalization have deepened interdependencies among social, economic, and political spheres (Benbya et al., 2020;OECD, 2019). In such systems, interactions among actors generate unpredictable dynamics, limiting the ability of policymakers to anticipate how these systems evolve (Geyer & Rihani, 2010). The problems governments face are similarly complex: they evolve over time, emerge from multiple interactions, and involve actors with divergent interests. Their ambiguity leaves room for multiple interpretations, such that evidence alone is insufficient to determine what should be done (Cairney, 2019). At the global level, new governance arrangements have emerged to address such problems, including multi-stakeholder partnerships, adding another layer of institutional complexity (Elsässer et al., 2025). Yet responses of this kind can prove counterproductive, raising the risk of wicked solutions that leave decision-makers with a system more complex than before (Peters et al., 2019). Within national systems, policies accumulate (Adam et al., 2019), often faster than public administrations expand their capacity to implement them (Fernández-i-Marín et al., 2024), while policy texts themselves add complexity through demanding language and connections to other legal instruments (Senninger, 2023). Complexity is therefore not only a feature of the environment policymakers face, but is also amplified by the responses they devise.Decades of research on complex problem solving and dynamic decision-making document persistent difficulties in understanding complex, dynamic environments (Dörner & Funke, 2017;Osman, 2010). Following Béchard et al. (2025), we use the wall of complexity as a descriptive label for the substantial deterioration in judgment and decision performance that can occur when decision-makers confront highly complex tasks. It does not denote a single or fixed threshold. Although capacity limits have been quantified for specific processes such as working memory and relational reasoning, the extent of this deterioration depends on task characteristics, individual differences, the strategies used, and the external support available. Among the many ways complexity has been described, we retain the three dimensions that bear most directly on cognitive demand: computational, relational, and dynamic complexity.Computational complexity arises when the number of possible ways to solve a problem grows so rapidly that exhaustive consideration becomes infeasible (Hélie & Pizlo, 2022). In politics, we see this in the multiplicity of actors, objectives, and policy instruments that can be combined. Because working memory holds only a few items at a time (Cowan, 2010), decision-makers can consider only a fraction of these possibilities.Relational complexity reflects how many interdependent variables must be integrated simultaneously to represent a problem (Halford et al., 1998). Performance drops substantially from three to four variables, and falls to chance level at five (Halford et al., 2005). Political decision-making routinely involves many more interacting elements, as governance networks connect numerous interdependent public, private, and nonprofit actors (Morçöl, 2023).Finally, dynamic complexity arises from feedback loops, time delays, and nonlinear relationships that shape how systems evolve (Sterman, 1994). Political decision-making reflects these dynamics, as choices made in one sphere of governance can alter decisions taken in another (Klijn & Snellen, 2009). Yet humans have particular difficulty understanding delayed feedback (Brehmer, 1992) and basic dynamic processes (Cronin et al., 2009).These forms of complexity impose demands that can exceed human cognitive capacities. How cognition adapts to them is therefore central to understanding political decision-making.Whether policymakers can escape the wall of complexity depends on a prior question: are they cognitively better equipped to withstand it than ordinary citizens (Béchard et al., 2025)? Although political science has often treated political elites as cognitively distinct from the public (Kertzer, 2022), experimental comparisons reveal few systematic differences in how elected officials and citizens process information and make judgments (Griffin, 2013;Vis & Stolwijk, 2022). This question also extends to the organizations in which policymakers work. Such organizations can increase their information-processing capacity by delegating routine matters to specialized units, allowing multiple issues to be handled in parallel. When a problem cannot be adequately addressed through established procedures, however, it requires central coordination and a sequential search for alternatives, making the limits of individual cognition more consequential (Jones, 2003).Organizations can therefore distribute and sometimes mitigate the demands of complexity, but they do not eliminate the human cognitive constraints associated with the wall. Political decision-making thus remains cognitively bounded (Cairney, 2019), requiring policymakers to simplify what they attend to, represent, and reason about.Policymakers face chronic information overload that exceeds what they can process (Walgrave & Dejaeghere, 2017). Since attention is a limited resource, they must allocate it selectively, focusing on a few problems at a time (Baumgartner et al., 2023). Part of this selection is delegated to staff, while the rest relies on heuristics that filter what merits processing (Walgrave & Dejaeghere, 2017). What fails this first filter never reaches the later stages of the decision-making process. Such filtering can also have representational consequences, making some interests more cognitively accessible than others and leaving decision-makers with an incomplete picture of those affected (Miler, 2009). Nor is what passes the filter necessarily represented accurately. Even when a problem is noticed, its severity may be underestimated. When deterioration occurs through small, routine changes, the reference point for judging the problem may gradually adjust, making its cumulative severity appear less urgent -a boiling frog dynamic that Epp and Thomas (2023) associate with slower policy responses.Mental models organize incoming information by selecting the variables and causal relationships deemed relevant, but tend to neglect accumulations, delays, feedback, and nonlinearities (Sterman, 1994). They further reduce complexity by grouping elements into larger units or processing them sequentially (Halford et al., 1998), so reasoning ultimately operates on a simplified representation rather than the full problem (Hélie & Pizlo, 2022).While simplification is useful for making complex tasks more tractable, it can also produce systematic errors in judgment (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974). Experimental evidence suggests that elected office does not insulate decision-makers from these errors. In a three-country study, elected representatives were strongly affected by gain-loss framing and status-quo presentation, and were more likely than citizens to continue investing in a failing program after substantial prior expenditure (Sheffer et al., 2018). Local councillors are similarly prone to conjunction errors and scope neglect (Stolwijk & Vis, 2021). Yet what matters for the quality of political decision-making is less the occurrence of these errors than the resistance of these errors to correction. Individuals readily detect distortions in the reasoning of others while judging their own conclusions to be sound (Pronin et al., 2002). Among politicians, additional evidence does not reduce, and can even increase, the influence of prior attitudes on how information is interpreted (Baekgaard et al., 2019). Requiring them to justify a decision has similar effect, strengthening motivated reasoning rather than tempering it (Christensen & Moynihan, 2024). Expertise and experience appear to offer little protection against such biases (Stolwijk & Vis, 2021). Despite reporting greater political knowledge, elected officials did not outperform the general population in a complex political simulation (Béchard et al., 2025).As the cognitive limits discussed above are structural, they cannot be eliminated, nor can decisionmakers overcome their effects on their own. The challenge is therefore to equip them to navigate complexity more effectively despite these constraints. We examine three ways of doing so: training decision-makers to reason about complex systems (Section 5.1), extending their capacities through human-AI collaboration (Section 5.2), and cultivating epistemic and regulatory humility about the limits of their judgment and of policy itself (Section 5.3).A first step is to develop systems thinking by learning to reason about the overall structure of a system or problem rather than its isolated elements (Fischer & Gonzalez, 2016). In our view, this should include an explicit understanding of key mechanisms of complexity, such as feedback, delays, nonlinear effects, and emergence. Complexity thinking provides an analytical lens for recognizing the evolving and partly unpredictable nature of these systems, and the resulting limits of prediction and control (Geyer & Rihani, 2010). The aim should be to foster what Funke (2022) calls complex systems literacy. Yet the dynamics of complex systems are often too counterintuitive to be inferred through unaided reasoning (Sterman, 2002). Merely thinking and talking about systems may therefore do little to reshape the mental models underlying decision-making, emphasizing the need for active modeling (Forrester, 2016). Although empirical evidence suggests that modelling used as a cognitive tool combined with explicit systems-thinking instruction can improve systems thinking (Hung, 2008), routinely building such models may be impractical for policymakers. We therefore see microworld simulations as a more accessible route to experiential training. These computerized environments incorporate key characteristics of complex systems while allowing participants to experiment with strategies and observe their consequences, without having to build the models themselves (Brehmer & Dörner, 1993). Microworlds have long been used to study complex and dynamic decision-making (Gonzalez et al., 2005), including in simulated governance environments, such as Ecopolicy (Lafond et al., 2012), and Democracy 3 (Béchard et al., 2025;Lafond et al., 2014).We see this as a promising foundation for extending their use to the training of policymakers. However, the effectiveness of such training depends on how the microworld is used rather than exposure alone (Sterman, 1994). Decision-making performance improves when training favours fewer, longer practice episodes over a greater number of short repetitions (Gonzalez, 2004), and when participants observe how an expert handles the task rather than reviewing their own decisions (Gonzalez, 2005). These findings, however, come from laboratory studies with university students, and whether skills acquired in microworlds transfer to real policy decisions remains to be established. And even if they do, training, however well designed, can change how a decision-maker approaches a system, but not eliminate the cognitive limits that constrain what they can process. That asymmetry is where tools designed to support decision-making become worth considering.Training can improve how decision-makers reason about complexity, but unaided cognition still has limits. A complementary approach is therefore to externalize part of the cognitive burden through decision-support technologies. Such tools can function as "cognitive prostheses," offloading part of the information-processing and representation demands onto external systems (Tremblay et al., 2017). AI considerably expands the possibilities for such cognitive support, not by providing decision-makers with more information, but by increasing their capacity to process and act upon it. It can support routine, information-intensive policy analysis (Wellstead et al., 2024), transform large volumes of raw data into decision-relevant information (Madanchian et al., 2026), and extend policy modelling by allowing decision-makers to test interventions before implementation (Margetts, 2022). Yet such cognitive support comes with a trade-off: the systems that help decision-makers navigate complexity can also shape how that complexity is perceived and judged. Algorithmic risk assessments, for example, can recast fundamental uncertainty as statistical risk (Hartmann & Wenzelburger, 2021), while AI-generated recommendations can become anchors for subsequent human judgments (Carter & Liu, 2025). More generally, cognitive vulnerabilities change with the degree of automation in the decision-making system: as human involvement decreases, risks shift from biases in human judgment toward excessive trust in the system and disengagement from the decision-making process (Van Rooy, 2024). These vulnerabilities mean that adding AI to human decision-making does not automatically lead to better decisions. Depending on how it is used and implemented, AI may mitigate some biases while reinforcing or creating others (Bertrand et al., 2022;Kliegr et al., 2021). AI may also relocate part of this complexity rather than reduce it, since machine-learning systems derive their outputs from high-dimensional computations that do not readily translate into humanly interpretable reasons (Burrell, 2016). Decision-makers who rely on systems they cannot fully understand can find it harder to answer for the decisions those systems inform, a difficulty that Grimmelikhuijsen and Meijer (2022) count among the threats to the legitimacy of algorithmic decision-making in government. We argue that these risks are not a reason to reject cognitive offloading, but to design human-AI collaboration more carefully. The challenge is therefore not to maximize AI involvement, but to design for complementarity between human and artificial cognition (Tremblay et al., 2026). Decision-support systems should make the goals, assumptions and uncertainties behind their recommendations intelligible to decision-makers, and allow these recommendations to be audited (Grisogono, 2020). This also requires AI systems specifically developed for public-policy contexts (Henderson et al., 2022), explicit allocations of human and algorithmic roles and degrees of autonomy (Simmler and Frischknecht, 2021), and anticipation of the organizational disruptions their implementation within governments creates (Tangi et al., 2025). Conceived in this way, human-AI collaboration could expand the ability of policymakers to navigate complexity beyond their natural capabilities, without replacing the judgment necessary for decision-making.There are several approaches to support human cognition; some are applied upstream, such as the development of systems thinking or the use of computer simulations, while others, such as AI, can enhance the decision-support tools used during the decision-making process itself. But these tools alone will not suffice, because training to deal with complexity involves not only acquiring new tools but also developing a certain form of epistemic humility. First and foremost, it involves recognizing that decision-making biases exist, that they have structural origins (Korteling et al., 2020), and that they influence our judgment even when we are aware of them (Pronin & Kugler, 2007). The next step is to be aware of the vulnerability of unaided human cognition in the face of complexity, and the need for support beyond individual effort alone. Jalonen's (2025) review recommends a humble approach, by recognizing that the properties of complex political-administrative systems make their evolution inherently difficult to predict and control. This mindset can be learned. Dunlop and Radaelli (2016) propose training practitioners in what they call regulatory humility, that is, questioning the limits of what can be regulated, recognizing that certain situations are partly beyond the control of public policy, and confronting their own illusions of control. Making policymakers aware of what, amid complexity, will always remain beyond their control is not an admission of powerlessness: it is the prerequisite for working around the wall rather than running into it.Political systems are becoming more complex. Under high complexity, the natural capacities of human cognition may no longer be sufficient for effective judgment and decision-making. Faced with this wall, policymakers adapt the way they process information by simplifying reality. Heuristics are a natural response, but they can also become a source of bias and errors in judgment. Suboptimal political decisions are therefore not necessarily a sign of individual incompetence but may also reflect cognitive mechanisms that reach their limits when confronted with high levels of complexity.We posit that the interaction between the universal limits of human cognition and the complexity of the contexts in which this cognition operates (Cairney & Weible, 2017) is an important, often overlooked, source of difficulty in political decision-making. We have proposed three complementary responses to this difficulty: developing systems thinking through training and simulations, extending decision-making capacity through human-AI collaboration, and cultivating the epistemic and regulatory humility needed to use both well. None of these responses removes the cognitive limits of policymakers, but together they can help them navigate complexity more effectively.

items.title: Agency now or later? Equity students' stories of learning with generative artificial intelligence
items.abstract: Many university students come from equity and diverse backgrounds; they often balance study with employment, caregiving, and health challenges. This chapter considers how students from equity backgrounds engage with generative artificial intelligence (GenAI). It draws on interview data, constructed as vignettes, and employs Emirbayer and Mische’s conception of practical-evaluative agency to explore how GenAI opens (or narrows) new trajectories of action for students. The analysis revealed that GenAI created options that were previously unavailable or misaligned with the students’ values or their perceived expectations. Their choices to engage with GenAI tools were typically oriented towards making progress under pressure. For students undertaking assessment tasks online and largely alone, GenAI operates as a mediating resource that provides rapid access to otherwise hidden or implicit information and offers immediate assistance with tasks. From this perspective, GenAI functions as an enabler of action in the moment. However, it may bypass interactions that contribute to learning and belonging. Rather than viewing GenAI use as inherently enabling or sacrificing, it may be more appropriate to see it as redistributing agency across time: expanding what is possible in the pressured present, while reshaping what is possible over longer timescales.

items.title: Agent Scrum: A sprint methodology for continuous software development by AI agent teams, with observations from 324 sprints
items.abstract: Agent Scrum keeps Scrum's core devices (a time-boxed sprint, a committed sprint backlog, story points, velocity, a Definition of Done and a retrospective) and rescales them for teams of AI coding agents. Sprints last two hours instead of two weeks; capacity comes from model rate limits instead of headcount; cost is measured as token velocity, the tokens consumed per merged story point. In the reference implementation, 79% of committed stories reached done inside the sprint (297 of 375 over 90 sprints), ceremony took under five minutes per sprint, and the human stakeholder spent under two hours a day. Working paper, version 0.1.

items.title: AgentDecept: Benchmarking Deceptive Behavior in Tool-Using LLM Agents under Pressure
items.abstract: LLM agents increasingly carry out multi-turn tasks across everyday applications, yet users often see only the agent's report rather than the observations, API calls, and state changes behind it. Existing deception benchmarks have studied long-horizon interactions and tool-use settings, but whether agents faithfully report their actions across realistic, stateful application workflows remains underexplored. To address this gap, we introduce AgentDecept, an executable benchmark for evaluating behavioral deception under pressure. AgentDecept contains 477 pressure variants derived from 257 source tasks across six pressure sources, each paired with a pressure-free counterpart. Interventions enter through event messages, task context, application state, tool responses, and service quotas, spanning explicit events and implicit task or environment changes. Our evidence-grounded protocol evaluates full trajectories by relating user-facing claims to time-ordered observations and executed outcomes, distinguishing falsification, concealment, and equivocation from honest failure and disclosed limitations. The resulting behavioral labels also provide a setting for testing existing activation-based probes. AgentDecept enables controlled analysis of when multi-turn agents' reports diverge from execution in realistic application interactions.

items.title: AgentHeal: Evaluating Goal-Preserving Resource Recovery of Web Agents under Access Barriers
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents have demonstrated strong capabilities in automating complex information-seeking and transactional tasks across the open web. However, their real-world reliability remains limited by access barriers, such as dead links, authentication walls, rate limits, and anti-scraping defenses. These barriers block the primary execution path, causing agents to abort prematurely, loop indefinitely, or quietly compromise the user's original constraints. Existing evaluations either implicitly assume that target resources are freely accessible or focus on transient perturbations that simple retries can resolve, failing to capture scenarios where agents must actively reroute around impassable bottlenecks. To bridge this gap, this paper introduces AgentHeal, a comprehensive benchmark evaluating goal-preserving resource recovery, defined as the ability of web agents to detect non-transient access barriers, pivot to legitimate alternative sources, and fulfill the user's exact original objective. Spanning nine barrier families across a counterfactual sandbox and real-website replay, our experiments on leading LLM backbones show that average task success drops sharply from 89.4% to 43.7% under access barriers. Further analysis reveals that agents frequently fall for deceptive look-alikes, fail to escalate to users when necessary, violate access policies, or waste computation on futile retries, providing actionable diagnostics for developing resilient web agents.

items.title: Agentic AI and Autonomous LLM Systems: A Scientific Literature Review
items.abstract: The shift of large language models (LLMs) from passive text generators to agentic systems marks a move toward autonomous intelligence. Agentic AI refers to systems that reason, plan, and execute actions in pursuit of complex goals with minimal human intervention. This paper reviews recent research on the architectural foundations, core functional modules, applications, and safety challenges of autonomous LLM systems. Current work emphasizes modular architectures in which an LLM serves as the central reasoning engine, augmented by components for perception, memory, planning, and tool interaction. Multi-agent systems have emerged as a dominant trend, enabling collaborative problem solving through structured orchestration and communication protocols. Although these systems show significant potential in software engineering, manufacturing, and cybersecurity, critical barriers remain in safety, reliability, and ethical governance. This review provides a structured overview of the state of the art and identifies key research directions for the coming years. Index Terms—agentic AI, autonomous agents, large language models, multi-agent systems, retrieval-augmented generation, tool use, AI safety

items.title: Agentic AI for Inclusive Assistive Ecosystems
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is transforming assistive technologies, yet many systems remain reactive, fragmented, and insufficiently personalized for individuals with disabilities and neurodivergent conditions. This chapter examines the architectural, design, and governance foundations of trustworthy agentic assistive systems. It synthesizes limitations of conventional approaches, including restricted adaptability, low interoperability, and weak support for user autonomy, and introduces a taxonomy of agentic architectures to guide scalable deployment. The chapter proposes a multi-agent framework integrating multimodal interaction, hybrid reasoning, explainable AI, and health-aware data to enable context-sensitive support. It further addresses privacy, ethical governance, and responsible institutional adoption while outlining future research directions. By bridging architectural innovation with human-centered design, this work advances a forward-looking vision for inclusive intelligent environments.

items.title: Agentic IoT for Urban Renewable Energy
items.abstract: This chapter examines agentic IoT as an emerging paradigm for renewable energy integration in smart cities. Conventional IoT architectures have improved urban energy monitoring and connectivity but remain largely reactive and rule-bound, insufficient for the coordination demands of distributed generation, intermittent supply, electrified mobility, and heterogeneous urban infrastructure. The chapter defines agentic IoT as an urban energy ecosystem in which connected devices, edge nodes, and digital platforms are embedded with situational awareness, dynamic decision-making, multi-agent coordination, adaptive learning, and bounded autonomous execution within predefined safety and policy constraints. A multi-layer conceptual framework is proposed, organized around physical energy assets, IoT sensing and actuation, data and digital twin capabilities, agentic intelligence, platform and ecosystem integration, and governance. The framework positions agentic IoT as an evolution beyond conventional and intelligent IoT toward more autonomous urban energy orchestration.

items.title: Agentic LLM reasoning in pediatric diabetes outcome prediction from multimodal medical records
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are proposed for clinical prediction but are untested in pediatrics, where cohorts are small and outcomes are uncommon. Using records from 2,489 youth with type 2 diabetes (T2D) and 4,018 with type 1 diabetes (T1D), spanning structured data, note-derived social determinants and, in T1D, continuous glucose monitoring data, we predicted seven T2D outcomes, four also in T1D, at 24 months from 18 months of follow-up. CEDAR (Clinical Evidence-Driven Agent for Risk-prediction), an evidence-citing, self-auditing LLM pipeline, outperformed trained machine learning in both cohorts (pooled area under the receiver operating characteristic curve 0.815 versus 0.656 to 0.700 in T2D and 0.756 versus 0.603 to 0.631 in T1D), most on the sparsely screened outcomes. Only 4 of 70,246 values it cited did not match the chart. Reading only the evidence and reasoning cited by CEDAR, two pediatric endocrinologists reached the same prediction as CEDAR in about nine of ten cases, agreeing with each other on 90.5%.

items.title: Agentic process evidence
items.abstract: The way software gets built is changing dramatically. AI agents now create pull requests, select dependencies, refactor codebases, interpret test failures, and execute infrastructure changes across the entire Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC). AI agents are autonomous team members, but unlike human engineers, they are ephemeral - their reasoning, decisions, and tool calls vanish the moment the session ends. Modern Security incidents involving intent mismatch or injection are becoming increasingly common - forcing us to address AI Agents as an insider threat. No widely adopted standard yet enables agentic provenance and governance and its obvious that you can't hold an ephemeral process accountable. The git log was designed for human commits. It shows what changed. It does not show what an AI agent did, which model it used, which tools it called, or whether anyone was accountable for the outcome. Every governance framework, every audit trail, every compliance control in the SDLC was built around one assumption: a human made the decision. That assumption no longer holds. This shift introduces 3 main procedural problems (not addressing scale) - Supply-chain vector - The agentic coder is software, so it is a supply-chain security risk. Policy guardrails - How to ensure the agentic coder is compliant with the policies of the organization. Task-alignment - How to align the agentic coder on its tasks and goals. We introduce Agentic Process Evidence (APE), a signed, tamper-evident, machine-readable attestation of agentic processes, linking the sessions to their outcome (process-aware logging). APE enables Policy-as-Code control over the agentic processes, allowing for human in the loop only when it's needed. We support the in-toto style attestation framework, and the protocol is aligned with the relevant regulations

items.title: Agentic University: Collaborative Agents for Personalized Learning
items.abstract: Large language models support personalized tutoring, content generation, and adaptive learning paths. However, capability development requires these resources and interactions to form a coherent learning process that evolves with the learner. A central challenge is to align goals, activities, and assessment while using learning evidence to decide what should follow. We introduce Human-Participatory Multi-Agent Organization and instantiate it in Agentic University (AU). In AU, learners participate as organization members and work with specialized agents to maintain a revisable Capability Program. The program connects personal goals, learning activities across modalities, and layered assessment, while learner feedback and performance guide subsequent support. Our evaluation shows advantages in program organization, assessment design, and revision quality. Users achieved larger mean assessment gains (12.19 versus 5.61 points on a 50-point scale) and reported stronger cognitive support. This work contributes an organizational approach to adaptive learning that makes learner participation a continuing basis for multi-agent coordination. The Agentic University project is available at \href{https://github.com/AgenticOrgLab/AgenticUniversity.git}.

items.title: AI and Immersive Technologies in Language Education
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) and immersive technologies are expanding opportunities for language learners to obtain feedback, revise writing, and rehearse communication. Their educational value depends on how these opportunities support learning and informed participation. Wu et al. (2025) locate recent technological developments within broader concerns about learner affect, teacher development, and immersive learning. This wider perspective is useful for understanding the nine articles in this special issue. Together, they examine how technological assistance interacts with critical thinking, authorship, communicative practice, and teacher agency. We bring these contributions into dialogue to consider the pedagogical conditions under which innovation supports learners’ developing capabilities.

items.title: AI and Machine Learning Approaches to Address Cybersecurity Challenges in Smart Grid Systems
items.abstract: Smart grid systems have been utilized with artificial intelligence (AI) which has substantially improved their efficiency and reliability. Nevertheless, with the development of smart grids into more intricate, networked, and data-intensive systems, a smart grid is becoming more susceptible to cybercrime. The chapter handles the problem of cybersecurity available within smart grid systems shedding light on the especial vulnerabilities that lies in the fact that they are digital and automated. It talks about the application of AI-based solutions to deal with such risks and it focuses on approaches that include anomaly detection, real-time threat responsiveness, and forecast risk. Besides, the chapter is also about AI aimed at protecting the communication network and providing more effective identification processes, and autonomic safe work. Through interpretation of case studies and projections in the real world, this paper gives a holistic idea of how AI can enhance the cybersecurity infrastructure in smart grid infrastructures.

items.title: AI and the double competence gap in dental education: towards symbiotic intelligence
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly becoming part of the knowledge infrastructure of healthcare. From diagnostic support and image interpretation to patient communication and clinical decision-making, AI-supported technologies, including generative AI, are changing the conditions under which healthcare professionals work. Dentistry is no exception. Recent research highlights emerging applications of AI in dental practice, while international reviews suggest growing opportunities and challenges associated with integrating AI into dental education. However, the rapid development of AI-supported technologies raises questions about how effectively professional education and continuing professional development can respond to evolving competency requirements. This raises a central question: How can dental education and continuing professional development respond to the potential double competence gap associated with AI-enabled dental practice?In this Opinion article, we address this question by proposing a conceptual framework that distinguishes between an initial education-practice gap and a continuing professional competence gap. Drawing on the concepts of AI literacy, Professional Digital Competence, and symbiotic intelligence, we discuss how dental education may develop and assess the competencies required for critical, ethical, and responsible AI use while preserving independent clinical reasoning, professional accountability, and patient-centred care.The rapid development of artificial intelligence raises important questions about how dental education can maintain the relevance of its curricula while safeguarding established standards of clinical competence, patient safety, and professional accountability. Although international reviews indicate growing interest in AI applications within dental education, systematic curricular integration appears to vary across institutions and educational contexts (9,10,24). Such variation should not necessarily be interpreted as resistance to technological change, as cautious implementation may also reflect legitimate concerns about educational quality, clinical validity, ethical safeguards, and the availability of robust evidence. Preliminary analyses of regulations and national curriculum frameworks for professional education raise questions about whether current educational provision adequately addresses emerging AIrelated competency requirements, potentially contributing to the two dimensions of the proposed double competence gap. Preliminary analyses of regulations and national curriculum frameworks for professional education suggest that this may contribute to reinforcing an already existing double competence gap When generative artificial intelligence became widely accessible through platform-based services such as ChatGPT in the autumn of 2022, many assumed that it would primarily affect the technology sector. However, when we tested a professional version of ChatGPT (GPT-4) in medicine, and partly in dental and psychology education, in March 2023, it was already apparent that this represented a technological paradigm shift with potentially farreaching implications across professional education programmes (1,2).While AI capabilities have developed rapidly in recent years in the health sciences (3)(4)(5)(6)(7)(8)(9)(10)(11), their integration into dental education presents a different set of challenges. Curriculum development, faculty preparation, assessment design, and clinical governance require careful consideration and cannot necessarily follow the pace of technological innovation. Recent reviews indicate that AI-related educational initiatives are emerging, but their integration into formal curricula and assessment practices remains variable. Several key explanations emerge from the literature: already overcrowded curricula, insufficient profession-specific digital competence among educators, and a lack of structured implementation (9,10,24). This potential misalignment between technological developments and structured educational provision provides an important rationale for examining the proposed double competence gap.Dental education has previously incorporated technologies such as digital radiography, simulation, intraoral scanning, and computer-aided design and manufacturing (29). These developments offer relevant lessons for AI integration: new technologies require faculty development, opportunities for supervised practice, alignment with clinical tasks, and assessment of what students can actually do. However, the current AI transition differs in its breadth and pace. Generative AI can be used across clinical reasoning, communication, learning, and assessment, including through tools that students access independently of their institutions. Moreover, the capabilities and limitations of these systems may change within a single curriculum cycle. Dental programmes should therefore draw on established approaches to curricular implementation while developing a more continuous process for reviewing AIrelated learning outcomes, teaching cases, and assessment practices.The Norwegian national curriculum regulations for healthcare professional education (RETHOS) emphasise that educational programmes should respond to society's current and future competence needs. However, AI is not explicitly addressed in the national curriculum regulations for dentistry, medicine, or psychology (12)(13)(14). Similarly, the Norwegian Agency for Quality Assurance in Education (NOKUT)'s national evaluation of medical education in 2025 provides limited explicit discussion of AI (15). These observations should be interpreted with caution. The absence of explicit AI terminology in national regulations or evaluation reports does not necessarily imply that AIrelated competencies are absent from institutional curricula, teaching practices, or assessment arrangements. National frameworks may deliberately emphasise enduring, technology-neutral professional competencies, allowing educational institutions to adapt their programmes to technological developments without requiring frequent regulatory revisions.Nevertheless, the limited explicit attention to AI in these national documents raises relevant questions about how emerging AI-related competencies are interpreted, operationalised, and assessed within individual educational programmes. International reviews have identified variation in the integration of AI into dental education, including challenges related to curriculum development, faculty preparedness, and the assessment of AI-related competencies (9,10,24).From the perspective of the proposed double competence gap framework, the central concern is therefore not simply whether AI is explicitly mentioned in national policy documents, but whether educational programmes systematically develop and assess the competencies required for responsible AI use in dental practice. Addressing this question requires empirical examination of institutional curricula, learning outcomes, educational activities, and assessment practices rather than relying solely on national policy analysis.Although the policy examples discussed here are drawn from Norway, the distinction between national competency frameworks, institutional curricula, and actual educational practices may also be relevant internationally. However, the extent to which the proposed double competence gap applies across different countries and dental education systems requires context-specific empirical investigation.The increasing integration of AI into healthcare knowledge infrastructures may also have epistemological implications for professional education. As AI systems become involved in information retrieval, diagnostic support, and clinical decision-making, questions arise concerning how professional knowledge is produced, evaluated, interpreted, and applied. These developments may gradually reshape aspects of professional roles and clinical reasoning, although their scope, pace, and educational consequences remain uncertain. Rather than predicting a specific timeline for such changes, dental education should develop adaptable approaches that enable students and practising professionals to critically evaluate emerging technologies while maintaining established standards of clinical expertise and professional accountability (16,18). Professional digital competence and AI literacy should become integral components of both the knowledge infrastructure and professional competence, and conceptual frameworks need to be developed that account for professionspecific AI use across both urban and rural patient contexts (17).At the same time, the challenge extends far beyond today's dentist education. The vast majority of today's practising professionals completed their education long before generative artificial intelligence became part of professional practice. Consequently, they have not necessarily received systematic training in how such AI systems can be used professionally, what their limitations are, or which ethical and legal challenges they may entail.We propose the concept of a double competence gap to describe two distinct but interconnected potential mismatches between the competencies required for responsible professional practice in increasingly AI-enabled dental healthcare and the competencies systematically developed through initial dental education and continuing professional development. A competence gap is understood here as a discrepancy between demonstrable professional capabilities and the knowledge, skills, and critical judgement required to perform relevant professional tasks safely, effectively, and ethically. Importantly, such gaps cannot be inferred solely from the availability of new technologies or the absence of explicit AI terminology in educational policy documents; their existence and extent require empirical investigation.The first competence gap, which we term the initial education-practice gap, concerns the potential misalignment between undergraduate dental education and the evolving competencies required in AI-enabled dental practice. International reviews suggest that the systematic integration of AI-related learning outcomes, teaching activities, and assessment practices in dental education remains uneven (9,10,24). This raises questions about whether existing educational provision adequately prepares students for the critical and clinically appropriate use of AI in future dental practice. Although students may independently engage with generative AI and other AI-supported technologies, such engagement does not necessarily constitute systematic development of profession-specific AI literacy. The central educational concern is therefore whether curricula, learning outcomes, teaching practices, and assessment arrangements adequately prepare students to critically evaluate AI-generated information, recognise its limitations, and integrate appropriate AI-supported decisionmaking with established clinical knowledge and professional judgement.The second competence gap, termed the continuing professional competence gap, concerns practising dentists whose initial professional education preceded the widespread availability of contemporary generative AI and other emerging AI applications. These professionals may encounter new technological expectations without having had equivalent opportunities for structured education in AI evaluation, clinical applicability, patient safety, data protection, and professional accountability. However, the extent of this gap is likely to vary across practitioners, clinical settings, previous digital experience, and access to continuing professional development.The conceptual contribution of the double competence gap framework lies in connecting these two educational challenges across the professional life course. Whereas AI literacy describes a set of relevant competencies, and Professional Digital Competence provides a broader perspective on technology-related professional capabilities, the double competence gap framework draws attention to the potential misalignment between competency requirements and educational provision at two different stages of professional development. It thereby offers a basis for examining how initial education, curriculum and assessment, faculty development, and continuing professional development can respond to changing professional requirements.We present the double competence gap as a conceptual and empirically testable proposition rather than as an established finding across dental education. Its educational significance depends on whether these proposed mismatches can be identified, assessed, and addressed in specific institutional and professional contexts.Empirically investigating the proposed double competence gap requires distinguishing between shortcomings in educational provision and demonstrable deficiencies in professional competence. The initial education -practice gap could be examined through curriculum mapping, IADT-guidelines (34IADT, 2026), analysis of intended learning outcomes and assessment practices, interviews with educators and students, and performance-based assessments of AI-related clinical competencies. The continuing professional competence gap could be investigated through research informed knowledge (33e.g. Ji et al., 2025), surveys, interviews, and scenario-based assessments involving practising dentists with different levels of professional experience and AI exposure. Importantly, the absence of explicit AI-related learning outcomes or structured training would indicate a potential gap in educational provision, but would not, in itself, demonstrate insufficient professional competence. Establishing a competence gap would require comparing observable performance with independently defined, clinically relevant competency standards, while accounting for differences in professional roles, practice contexts, and access to continuing professional development.Addressing the proposed double competence gap requires conceptual clarity regarding AI literacy, Professional Digital Competence (PDC), and symbiotic intelligence (SI). items.title: AI at a Turning Point: From ChatGPT through Neural Networks to Neuromorphic AI
items.abstract: The tension between the established technologies of connectionist AI and their neuromorphic challengers is attracting growing attention, above all because of the enormous energy demand of the former and the low power consumption of the latter. Developing and running large AI models consumes gigawatt- to terawatt-hours of energy, while the human brain operates on a continuous 20 watts. Spiking neural networks (SNNs) counter this energy demand with a frugal approach and bring elements of self-organization into the methodological repertoire of AI: local learning instead of global error backpropagation, event-driven computing, and time as a carrier of information. They do not replace today's AI but extend it; in hybrid systems each approach can be deployed where its strengths lie. This monograph explains the field in a generally accessible yet mathematically rigorous way. Using the text-generation module of ChatGPT as an example, the principle, elegance, and computational cost of transformer-based AI are presented and compared with the coding, learning, and network-design methods of SNNs. Throughout, relevant mechanisms of the human nervous system serve as model and reference point. Topics include spike-timing-dependent plasticity, population and temporal coding, the Neural Engineering Framework, neuromorphic hardware from Loihi 2 to commercial edge processors, and the prospects for classical and neuromorphic AI to complement and extend each other.

items.title: AI CHAT ASSISTANT FOR ONLINE BUSINESS
items.abstract: Online businesses must answer product questions, explain policies, guide purchases and resolve order-related concerns across multiplechannels. Human-only support can be costly and slow during peak demand, while rigid rule-based chatbots struggle with varied wording andmulti-step questions. This paper presents a conceptual design for an Artificial Intelligence (AI) Chat Assistant for Online Business thatcombines natural language understanding, retrieval from approved business knowledge, controlled access to commerce services andescalation to human staff. The proposed assistant interprets customer intent, retrieves relevant product and policy information, generatesgrounded responses, and invokes permitted actions such as checking order status only after appropriate authentication. The architectureemphasizes factual consistency, privacy, security, accessibility and measurable service quality. It also describes a developmentmethodology, evaluation metrics, risk controls and a staged deployment plan. Since this is a design-oriented study, no original performanceresults are claimed; the proposed evaluation must be conducted using representative customer queries and verified business data.

items.title: AI Chatbot-Assisted Teaching and Student Learning Outcomes
items.abstract: The instructional effectiveness of artificial intelligence (AI) dialogue tools in higher education varies across contexts and depends on multiple moderation mechanisms. This structured evidence synthesis of eight studies identifies four moderation dimensions: task embedding depth, feedback granularity, teacher orchestration intensity, and discipline verification pressure. These dimensions are examined through task cycles, feedback characteristics, teacher intervention, and verification requirements. The findings show that higher intensity configurations with structured task embedding, layered feedback, teacher orchestration, and content verification are associated with higher composite coding indices across learning gains, engagement, trust, and knowledge transfer. A four-stage closed-loop learning pathway is proposed to support the pedagogical integration of AI dialogue tools. The findings highlight the importance of moderation mechanisms, teacher orchestration, and feedback granularity in designing effective AI-supported learning environments.

items.title: AI Cosmos: An Agentic Infra for Situated Learning
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can improve task performance during learning, yet these gains do not necessarily reflect learners' ability to thereafter apply the knowledge and skills independently. We present AI Cosmos, an agentic infrastructure for situated learning that organizes learning around two complementary principles: scenario-based participation and cumulative assets of practice. AI Cosmos organizes learners and role-specialized agents within learning scenarios that integrate task-relevant knowledge and, when needed, executable workbenches. An asset-memory loop preserves the processes and outcomes of practice as reusable assets with explicit provenance and dependencies. We evaluate scenario-based interaction through two preregistered randomized controlled studies examining the acquisition of legal reasoning and programming competence, holding the same underlying LLM across conditions. AI Cosmos achieves greater learning gains than a conventional LLM in legal reasoning and higher mastery of unseen programming problems than an LLM-as-Teacher baseline.

items.title: AI for Science in Space: Orbital Laboratories, Planetary Fieldwork, and Embodied Autonomy
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence for science (AI4S) is extending from interpretation of existing data to the design and execution of experiments. Space offers distinctive scientific opportunities while restricting physical support. Microgravity and extraterrestrial environments expose phenomena that terrestrial experiments cannot fully reproduce; finite samples, constrained resources, and limited opportunities for intervention complicate sustained investigation. This critical review examines orbital laboratories and planetary in situ science across biology, materials, fluid and thermal physics, and adaptive exploration. We distinguish learning from space-derived data, selecting scientific actions, executing them, and preserving experimental validity. Terrestrial self-driving laboratories provide complementary evidence on optimization, dedicated automation, robotic manipulation, and the support needed for unattended operation. The synthesis connects scientific gains already demonstrated by bounded AI systems to gaps in observation, executable actions, and continuity of valid evidence. Space robots can expand the attainable scope of autonomous science when necessary interventions exceed validated instrument capabilities and timely human support is unavailable. Their value must be established against dedicated mechanisms, redundancy, and human-supported operation. We develop a framework connecting sample history, scientific decisions, physical execution, and claim-specific validity. A worked orbital design, a planetary extension, and matched evaluation schemes separate the contributions of sensing, decision policies, and physical actions. The resulting agenda measures autonomy through valid scientific return, task coverage, intervention costs, and evidence integrity across complete campaigns.

items.abstract: For this study, we first did an assessment of students’ motivation for HE and their academic experience so far; we then examined university students’ perceptions of the use Artificial Intelligence in their formal learning. The participants were students enrolled into different courses at Cosmopolitan university, Abuja. This research survey examines university students’ perceptions of the use Artificial Intelligence in their higher education learning. A descriptive survey research method was used. Specifically, a questionnaire was used to collect data. The participants were students enrolled in different courses at Cosmopolitan university in Abuja, Nigeria. The results showed that the participants had positive perceptions of the use Artificial Intelligence in their university learning in affective, cognitive, and cognitive domains. Students’ perceptions of the use Artificial Intelligence in their university learning did not differ significantly according to perceived digital dependency. However, students’ perceptions of the use Artificial Intelligence in their university learning were influenced by their use of some AI tools and perceived digital competency. Future directions based on the findings were presented

items.title: AI in the EGI e-infrastructure -- Past experiences and future strategies
items.abstract: The EGI Federation has provided federated e-infrastructure services to European and global science for over 15 years. We review EGI's early experiences with AI in the interTwin and iMagine Horizon Europe projects, which built digital twins in physics and environmental sciences and an image-analysis platform for aquatic research. We then examine how the AI landscape has changed since 2023 and argue that the focus of AI in science has shifted from model training to adapting and applying AI to specific domains, projects and questions. Building on these lessons, we present the AI strategy emerging from the EGI Federation Strategy 2026-2030, organised around three enablers: (1) an AI-ready infrastructure connecting compute, data and application resources across the continuum; (2) human skills to know what is possible with AI and how to implement it; and (3) trust, to run AI with confidence even in high-risk environments. We describe the projects implementing each enabler, including federated LLM inference, AI-ready data platforms and AI competence centres, and discuss a division of labour with EuroHPC's AI Factories, RAISE, research infrastructures and EOSC, in which EGI specialises in the customisation and long-term operation of AI for research.

items.title: AI Literacy and Migrant Rights Information in Bangladesh: A Survey of AI Aware Respondents
items.abstract: Accurate and accessible information can help people navigating overseas employment, while generative artificial intelligence (AI) creates new questions about the quality and verification of migration-related advice. This study examines responses to statements about AI literacy and migrant-worker-rights information in 385 adult, AI-aware survey records from Bangladesh. The mixed sample includes law students, graduates, legal professionals and other respondents; prospective overseas workers are not identified in the workbook. The questionnaire asks about self-reported ability to locate rights information with AI, recognition of the need to verify migration information, awareness of misleading recruitment information and support for pre-departure AI-literacy training. It does not test knowledge of specific migrant-worker rights or observe use of an AI migration service. Item distributions, joint endorsement, paired comparisons and exploratory ordinal correlations are reported. Of 385 respondents, 256 (66.5%) endorsed the ability-to-locate statement, 341 (88.6%) endorsed the need to verify AI-generated migration information, and 267 (69.4%) supported AI-literacy training in pre-departure preparation. A total of 231 respondents (60.0%) endorsed both locating information and the need for verification; 110 endorsed verification without endorsing locating information. These answers do not establish actual verification or training effectiveness. The article distinguishes locating information, verifying its authority, knowing a legal right and obtaining an effective remedy. Future research should identify prospective workers, use rights-specific scenarios and document recruitment and consent procedures.

items.title: AI Universal Design for Learning and Inclusive Teaching Practices
items.abstract: This chapter explores the integration of artificial intelligence (AI), universal design for learning (UDL), and inclusive teaching practices in higher education to enhance institutional performance. It examines how AI supports personalised learning, accessibility, and differentiated instruction aligned with UDL principles. Using conceptual analysis, the chapter shows that inclusive teaching improves engagement, retention, and equitable outcomes. It also situates inclusive pedagogy within social justice frameworks. Findings indicate that AI strengthens flexibility and responsiveness, while UDL promotes proactive accessibility for diverse learners. However, challenges such as algorithmic bias, data privacy, and unequal access remain critical considerations.
